articles.title: Australian TikTok statistics to inform your 2026 strategy
articles.fullContent:
Known and beloved for its compelling short-form video content, TikTok has become a social powerhouse in Australia. According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, 39% of Australian social users turn to TikTok to keep up with trends in many areas, from finance to fashion, technology to travel. For businesses, this level of engagement represents a major marketing opportunity—but only if they know exactly how and why Australians are using the app.

The latest TikTok statistics in Australia point to an app whose role keeps shifting. What started as an entertainment feed now shapes how Australians discover products, research big decisions and connect with the brands they love. Marketers who understand that shift meet their audience where attention already lives and turn casual scrolling into real business results.

In this guide, we cover the most important TikTok statistics in Australia to help you build a smarter, data-led strategy. With these insights, you can guide your social strategy, spark TikTok campaign ideas and create content that truly resonates with Australian audiences.

Key TikTok statistics in Australia

TikTok is a major player in Australia’s social media landscape. As of late 2025, 10.9 million Australians aged 18 and over use the app, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report. These statistics show how deeply the network has embedded itself into everyday life:

  • More than 350,000 Australian businesses use TikTok, restated by the company in 2026.

  • Australian users spend an average of 1 hour 14 minutes a day in the app (August 2025), the highest daily figure of any social app in Australia, per DataReportal and We Are Social.

  • Per a Deloitte report, Australian TikTok users spend most of their time on the app watching videos, listening to audio and browsing feeds.

  • According to Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report, short-form videos (<60 seconds long) perform best on TikTok. Users are most interested in entertaining content, product discovery and influencer partnerships

With Sprout Social, you can schedule TikTok posts, track performance and spot emerging trends from the same platform you use to manage every other network.

The rise of TikTok in Australia: TikTok stats on growth in the Australian market

Although it’s been a major player in Australia’s social media landscape for years, TikTok is constantly evolving. What primarily began as an entertainment platform has transformed into a source of information, an outlet for cultural connection and a driver for social change.

  • In Q4 2024 alone, TikTok generated 186 million downloads from users globally.

  • TikTok ads reached 51.2% of Australian adults aged 18 and over at the end of 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • TikTok’s ad reach grew 13.9% year-on-year in Australia, adding 1.33 million users, the fastest growth of any major Australian platform, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Australia counted 21.0 million social media user identities in October 2025, equal to 77.7% of the population, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to a 2024 report from Oxford Economics, 19% of Australian users have donated to a charity or cause they saw on TikTok, and 18% have committed their time to volunteer.

TikTok Australia user and demographic statistics

TikTok appeals strongly to younger audiences; over 30% of its global audience is aged 18–24. Given that young people are Australia’s most active social shoppers, TikTok is an ideal platform for brands to connect with and sell to these users. From gender to income, here’s a more in-depth look at Australian TikTokers:

  • Around 74% of TikTok’s Australian user base is younger than 34, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to Statista, around 53.1% of Australians aged 18 and over use TikTok.

  • 72% of Gen Z have TikTok accounts, compared with 50% of users overall, per Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report.

  • Almost half (48%) of Australians aged 18 to 24 use TikTok to get news, per the University of Canberra’s Digital News Report 2026.

  • According to Statista, TikTok is more popular with Gen Z than other social networks.

  • TikTok’s adult advertising audience in Australia was 53.6% male and 46.4% female in late 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Further, the 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report reveals that 37% of Millennials globally have TikTok accounts.

  • A 2024 survey found that 41% of Gen Z shoppers had made purchases through social media in the past six months, followed closely by Millennials (40%).

  • Statista reports that, while Millennials favour Facebook for social shopping, Instagram and TikTok attract more Zoomers.

Australia’s social media ban for children under 16 reshapes this picture. It removes under-16s from the platform, which shifts TikTok’s Australian audience even further towards adults. Here’s what that means for your strategy.

How does Australia’s under-16 social media ban affect TikTok?

Australia’s under-16 social media ban took effect on 10 December 2025 under the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2024. It requires TikTok and nine other social media platforms to take reasonable steps to stop Australians under 16 from holding accounts, with fines of up to A$49.5 million for non-compliance, per the eSafety Commissioner.

  1. Social media optimization improves reach, engagement, and conversions. It works by refining your profiles, content, and posting strategy based on data, not guesswork.

What is social media optimization?

Social media optimization is the process of improving your social media content, profiles, and strategies to achieve better results: faster follower growth, higher levels of engagement, more clicks or conversions, and so on.

SMO covers both the small, tactical improvements you make to individual posts and the bigger strategic decisions behind your presence, like which platforms you invest in and what your content mix looks like.

Common tactics of social media optimization include:

  • Basic improvements to individual posts, such as adding a call-to-action in a caption or picking a scroll-stopping visual
  • Larger strategic improvements, like redefining your brand’s tone of voice on social media
  • Optimizing posting times and frequency based on audience behavior
  • Improving discoverability, such as adding keywords to bios and captions so your content surfaces in social search

That last point matters more each year. Social platforms increasingly function as discovery and search engines, so optimization is no longer just about pleasing a feed algorithm. It’s about being findable.

And because platforms like TikTok and Instagram now behave like search engines themselves, many of the same habits apply: research what people are looking for, use their language, and structure content so it’s easy to categorize.

In short, treat SMO and SEO as two halves of the same discoverability strategy rather than competing channels.

With nearly 5.75 billion social media users worldwide in 2026, social media optimization helps your content reach the right people and actually perform once it gets in front of them.   • Sell more products or services: Clear messaging and stronger engagement can turn attention into sales.

Google’s new Preferred Sources embed removes one action from the process of adding a publication as a Preferred Source.

With the embed, a reader adds the site and returns to the article. A deeplink sends the reader to Google’s source preferences tool, where the site still has to be selected and confirmed.

This simple guide shows how to add the button to your website and provides WordPress widget code you can use.

What Google’s Preferred Sources Feature Does

Preferred Sources affects what an individual Google user sees after selecting your publication. It does not improve your site’s rankings for everyone or guarantee that your articles will appear in Top Stories .

According to Google’s documentation , it is available globally for Top Stories in the languages where Google Search is available. Preferred sources can also be highlighted in AI Overviews and AI Mode where those experiences are available.

See also: Google’s Liz Reid: Personalization Can Help Small Publishers

Check Eligibility Before You Add The Button

First, search for your publication in Google’s source preferences tool . If it does not appear there, adding the button will not solve the eligibility issue.

Google supports domains and subdomains, but not subdirectories. These are valid targets:

If the publication lives on a subdomain, use that host rather than assuming the root domain is interchangeable.

Add The Standard Preferred Sources Button

Google recommends its standard JavaScript implementation because it is localized automatically and returns the reader to the page where they started.

Standard Button Vs. Deeplink: What I Observed

I tested both routes on mobile. With the embedded button, Google opens a publication-specific confirmation page. The source is already identified, the reader taps Add , and Google returns them to the article. After the initial click on your website, it is a single-action flow.

The deeplink is different. It opens the general Source preferences screen with the publication search filled in, but the reader still has to select the publication’s checkbox. Google also does not automatically return them to the article. In practice, the embed removes one extra action, so it creates less friction.

articles.title: Social media automation: A 3-step quick start guide for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Between all the DMs you need to answer and the posts you need to create, it’s time-consuming to maintain an active social media presence. And as you expand to more channels without increasing headcount, you get sucked into a productivity trap where you’re doing more work, but your results stagnate.

This is all too familiar for social media teams that do (almost) everything manually. The Social Media Productivity Report from Sprout Social even found that 63% of are unable to do high-impact work because they’re bogged down by manual tasks.

On the other hand, respondents who use dedicated tools to manage their social media are twice as likely to have enough time to get their work done.

This makes a strong case for marketers to start automating various aspects of their social media management. In this social media automation guide, we break down three essential steps to get started. Let’s take a look.

What social media automation means

Social media automation is the process of letting tools handle routine and repetitive tasks like scheduling posts or tracking brand mentions. This gives you back the time needed for more meaningful work that requires human input, whether that’s responding to your DMs or creating high-quality content.

Rather than “replacing you,” automation allows you to free up time by automating the routine. So you have more time to spend on personalizing the meaningful.

Step 1: Centralize your publishing

Connect your profiles to one dashboard

You waste time when you’re manually logging into different profiles to schedule every post individually. Streamline the process by connecting all your social media profiles to a centralized publishing dashboard.

A social media management platform like Sprout consolidates your publishing through a single dashboard. This lets you connect your profiles across different social networks and manage your publishing in one place. When you create a new post to schedule, all you have to do is select the profile(s) where you want to publish it.

Build a lightweight content calendar

Before all the automation comes the planning. And you need to plan your posts ahead of time before you can schedule them.

A content calendar makes it easy to do this and organize your publishing efforts. When you already have content planned for the entire week or month, you can quickly start creating posts without spending too much time on ideation.

And you don’t have to build an elaborate calendar, either. Keep it simple with a clear outline of the essentials:

  • Publishing date and time
  • Platform and profile
  • Content pillar or topic
  • Format

Sprout’s content calendar helps you visualize your planned posts across all your profiles. It lets you create and schedule posts directly within the calendar, which simplifies your publishing automation. You can even drag and drop posts to easily adjust your publishing cadence for optimal frequency.

Schedule around optimal send times

Effective publishing automation is highly strategic. It’s less about the publishing volume and more about the timing precision. When you schedule your posts to automatically go live, you need to time them to make sure they reach audiences when they’re most active.

Sprout’s social media automation features like Sprout Queue let you do just that. It automatically sends out your posts at a time of your choosing, so you no longer have to set reminders to remember when it’s time to post. You can schedule posts in bulk and for the entire month, freeing up time to focus on more high-impact tasks.

ViralPost™ takes the guesswork out of scheduling with optimal send time recommendations. It analyzes your audience and their engagement patterns to figure out when to deliver content for the greatest impact.

Step 2: Set up automated engagement and response rules

Unify your inbox across platforms

Many social media managers still handle engagement manually because they want to keep it human. But there are other aspects of engagement that you can automate without losing the human touch.

This starts with the process of tracking your comments, DMs and brand mentions. Instead of tracking everything manually across different networks and profiles, you can automatically collect them in a centralized inbox. This unifies all your engagement opportunities, so nothing falls through the cracks.

Sprout’s Smart Inbox centralizes all your messages from across your connected profiles. This helps you keep up with the latest comments and DMs without having to manually open your social media app. It even lets you manage your responses directly within the inbox.

Automated Inbox Rules further help you manage your responses more efficiently by measuring and categorizing inbound messages. So it’s easy to see which messages you need to prioritize and which ones can wait for a bit.

Build FAQ-style auto-responses for common questions

Quick response times make brands stand out on social. According to the 2025 Sprout Social Index™, nearly three-quarters of consumers expect a response within 24 hours. And 73% will even buy from a competitor if a brand doesn’t respond on social.

But manually answering every message or question slows you down. While this keeps your brand human, it means people have to wait longer even for a generic question. That’s the part of engagement you can automate, giving you more time to focus on interactions that need a more tailored response.

Sprout’s Bot Builder lets you create chatbots and automate responses for frequently asked questions. This streamlines your X (Twitter) and Facebook automation efforts to speed up responses and field routine customer care enquiries.

By Mark Mwachiro Top of the Ticker : Regular CNN viewers were greeted with pixelated images during the noon ET hour on Monday as the network suffered a technical issue that affected audio and video.

The technical issues occurred during a panel discussion on Inside Politics with Dana Bash , forcing the network to go temporarily off air. The interruption lasted more than 30 minutes, which CNN acknowledged in a social media post.

On-air tribute : Noticias Telemundo anchor Julio Vaqueiro will host a primetime special tribute to the late Mexican musical icon Juan Gabriel on Friday at 10 p.m. ET. Airing live on Telemundo and streaming on Noticias Telemundo Ahora, Juan Gabriel, Amor Eterno will feature in-depth interviews with family and friends as they reflect on Gabriel’s life and his prolific 45-year musical career, encompassing more than 1,500 songs released across more than 40 albums. In this new role, Simmons will report to Marie Beaudette , vice president, business and media for CNN.

An executive with more than 15 years of fundraising experience, Hixon-Day has previously worked at the Smithsonian Institution as chief advancement officer and as vice president of development at the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

articles.title: A Retailer’s Checklist to Prevent the Next Target Costume Blunder
articles.fullContent:
By Nataly Kelly The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

In 2020, Target pulled a children’s costume from its website after shoppers pointed out that it evoked Anne Frank . Six years later, the retailer is apologizing again, this time for a children’s Halloween costume that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

Target responded in typical corporate fashion. It pulled the product, apologized, and promised internal reviews of the situation. But we all know that the veil of proactivity fades in favor of waiting for all of the uproar to blow over.

When does an apology stop being a checkbox exercise as opposed to a genuine learning moment?

A massive corporation like Target no doubt has checks, balances, and stage gates for almost everything. And there’s real volume and pressure behind seasonal innovation.

Target has said some of its strongest recent performance has come in the fall, and nearly 70% of its Halloween assortment this year is new. That’s a lot of innovation moving through an organization quickly.

One offensive product is a mistake; two is a concerning trend.

When a similar failure happens again, it raises a harder question: What did the organization actually learn the first time?

The bar is high and teams are stretched thin trying to find ideas that land. Products are tested for risk—things like choking, flammability, sizing, cost. What’s too often disconnected is how an individual product might affect perception of the brand.

There is no innovation without brand, and no brand without innovation. But the teams tasked with each are often operating separately.

Classify products by their potential for brand risk

A costume carries fundamentally different risks than a towel or a blender. Costumes regularly venture into the territory of culture, identity and at times, appropriation. In a Talker Research survey of American parents, 29% said costumes built around cultural stereotypes should be pulled from stores. For anything involving blackface, that number rose to 43%. Some lines are clearer than others. Seasonal deadlines make that scrutiny harder, but also more important.

Teams need to look at the composite, not just the individual components. In the Target example, a children’s striped bodysuit alone reads as a clown suit. Add a black mesh mask with a snaggletoothed grin. Then add black gloves and a tiny top hat with a flower on the brim. Most companies review the tech pack and never review the photograph of the image, but the photograph is what the customer ultimately sees, and reacts to.

Before this conversation exploded on social media, shoppers were already flagging the costume in Target’s own product reviews. That’s the kind of signal companies spend enormous amounts of money trying to find. Another problem is often that the people moderating product reviews don’t talk to the people creating products, and most of those folks are not getting feedback directly from consumers whatsoever. In a hundred-thousand-person company, things fall through the cracks. Consumer research only helps if it can travel horizontally across the organization, and can be accessed quickly enough for every employee making a decision that affects the brand to act on it. At many companies, access to consumer testing is not yet democratized and widely available.

Address the cultural problems no checklist can solve.

No one wakes up hoping to destroy brand equity and alienate consumers. Companies repeat mistakes when they treat their own response as a project with an end date instead of a system that has to be built and maintained for the long term.

Think about what six years does to an organization the size of Target. The team that felt the heat in 2020 is gone. The vp that commissioned the internal review may have retired. The consultant that curated the design invoiced and moved on. The task force fizzled out not long after the news cycle. And the document with the retro is still sitting in a drive nobody opens under a name that no longer has any relevance.

That requires better consumer feedback and more connected data. But no amount of testing can make up for one cold, hard fact. Somebody who could have looked at this costume and immediately seen the problem was either not involved, or wasn’t heard early enough to stop it.

Target will recover, and eventually the news cycle will move on, as it goes. But while consumers can look past a mistake, it’s very hard to undo how a brand made them feel. The goal shouldn’t be to get better at apologizing. It’s to build an organization that remembers why it had to apologize in the first place, and keeps the next embarrassing mea culpa from happening.

Nataly Kelly is the chief marketing officer of Zappi.

articles.title: Reddit statistics in 2026 and tactics to grow your brand
articles.fullContent:
Reddit spent years as the internet’s best-kept secret. In 2026, the secret’s out. It’s one of the web’s fastest-growing platforms and a primary source powering AI search results. The conversations happening inside its communities shape what your customers read everywhere else.

That shift changes the math for marketers. Use these current Reddit statistics to benchmark your audience, understand user behavior and refine your Reddit marketing strategy.

Here’s what the latest data makes clear:

  • Reddit crossed 514.6 million weekly active uniques for the first time in Q2 2026, with daily active uniques up 18% year over year. Its audience is scaling fast, so early movers still have room to build authority.

  • The US is Reddit’s largest single market at 194.8 million users and 42.95% of traffic, but international daily users now outpace it. Your reach here isn’t capped by borders.

  • Only 22% of social users have a Reddit profile, yet the platform’s influence runs far deeper than that number suggests. Lurkers and searchers, not just registered accounts, drive its reach.

Reddit user demographics statistics

  • 48% of US adults who use Reddit are between 18–29 years old, followed by 30–49-year-olds.

  • As of 2026, 59.8% of users identified as male and 39.7% as female.

  • In 2025, US users’ ethnicities were 27% White, 18% Black, 22% Hispanic and 44% Asian.

  • Reddit’s largest audiences outside the US are in the UK (45.8 million), Canada (43.1 million), India (30.8 million), Germany (29.3 million) and Australia (23.3 million).

  • International daily users (77.1 million) now outpace US daily users (53.2 million) and are growing around 28% a year.

Reddit’s users lean young, making it a valuable social media platform for reaching Gen Z and younger millennials. While it reaches US audiences well, India, the United Kingdom and Canada also have notable bases.

These data points reveal a unique advantage for brands targeting social media demographics like Reddit’s through authenticity, community engagement and value-first organic interactions.

Targeting niche subreddits lets you focus on high-intent topics. Localized subreddits also allow teams to tailor campaigns by city or country.

Use these demographic insights to build a targeted Reddit marketing strategy that connects with high-intent audiences.

How Reddit users engage: Understanding behavior and traffic

On Reddit.com, you can increase engagement in a few ways. People spot your post or comment in their feed, or find you inside a specific subreddit. The other big driver is search engines.

Reddit is a popular place for real information. Because of Google’s $60 million yearly deal with Reddit and how people search, many internet users find Reddit posts through search engines.

Here are the key Reddit traffic and behavior numbers driving that discovery:

  • As of Q2 2026, Reddit reached over 130 million active daily users—77.7 million logged out and 52.6 million logged in.

  • That means 59.7% of daily users browse Reddit while logged out.

  • Organic search sends roughly 66.88% of Reddit’s traffic, which is exactly why that Google deal matters.

  • More than 80 million people search directly on Reddit each week.

  • Reddit has 2.3 billion backlinks from 1.4 million referring domains.

Foundation Marketing’s analysis of Reddit stats reveals key post performance benchmarks:

  • Titles between 160–180 characters earned the most upvotes.

  • The performance gap between question and non-question titles is now statistically negligible, under 1%.

  • Longer, descriptive titles consistently outperform very short ones.

Reddit user behavior & community norms

  • Redditors engage with authenticity: Reddit user behavior is often different from users on other social media platforms. They are invested in in-depth discussions about other people’s genuine thoughts, opinions and perspectives. Because of this, they’re invested in authentic discussions and are skeptical of promotional language and overt marketing.

  • All users are expected to respect subreddit rules and guidelines: Each subreddit has its own rules, guidelines and styles of engagement that all users are expected to follow. If you break those standards, you could easily lose trust, especially as a marketer. As a marketer, it’s important to understand community nuances and learn how users talk and think in the niche communities you’re involved in.

  • Users trust the authenticity of product reviews on Reddit: Since Reddit is a community-based platform, what users organically say about a product or business carries weight. To engage with redditors successfully, brands must join conversations and add enriching perspectives. And to maintain credibility across subreddits, avoid direct promotional pitches.

  • Redditors especially engage in the comments: The real value for users lies in the comment section of posts. Users have countless conversations that rabbit trail from the original post’s initial discussion. Your brand can hop into the myriad of conversations within just one thread and build relational equity within that community.

articles.title: Don’t Let Retail Media Tell You It’s Brand Building
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Ritson Walmart’s second-quarter earnings call on Aug. 20 was more like a party . You’d be breaking out the hats and noisemakers too if your global advertising revenue was up 38%. Walmart Connect, its U.S. retail media arm, posted even higher gains of 43%.

The scale of that growth is staggering. In 2025, Walmart made $713 billion with $6.4 billion coming from advertising, up 46% year-over-year. That might only represent 1% of Walmart’s revenue, but consider that its advertising arm alone is nearly as big as a retailer like Ralph Lauren’s entire business .

And remember that’s retail revenue, not profit. Walmart’s retail business operates at around a 4% margin. Retail media is a much more profitable pursuit, typically operating at around 70% margin. So the profit numbers tell a very different story.

That’s why Bentonville is so enthused about its ad business. And it’s growing at a rate like nothing else on its books.

Walmart is just the most prominent example of the ongoing retail media revolution. Target reported $915 million in advertising revenue last year, up from $522 million two years earlier, even as it reported three years of flat or falling sales. Instacart and DoorDash each clear about a billion dollars a year selling ads inside food-delivery apps. And of course there is Amazon, whose ad business took in $76 billion over the last 12 months and holds just under 80% of the U.S. retail media market.

The store business is mostly flat. The ad business is not.

Retail media is nothing new. It’s slotting fees with a fancy name and a dashboard. Ever since the 1980s, brands have been paying retailers for a whole raft of favors: shelf position, end caps, gondola ends, and the distinct privilege of not being delisted.

Retail media just represents its natural evolution. And like slotting fees, none of the manufacturers paying into the retail media machine are going to complain about it. Quite the opposite.

P&G CEO Shailesh Jejurikar recently described retail media as an opportunity that will “enable our brands to create value across all retail formats.” I’m sure in private he loves reallocating millions from his brand-building budgets so Walmart and Target will do what they used to do for free. But nobody, not even P&G, messes with big retail. So for now, the retail marketing business keeps growing and everyone is “happy” with the “opportunity.”

But scratch the surface of retail media, and problems are brewing. First, there is ROI and the utter incomparability of ad performance across retailers. Jackson Bazley, the ANA’s head of measurement, describes comparing performance across retail networks as “evaluating purple to bananas to 9.7 stars.” Good luck asking notoriously private, self-serving behemoths to unite around a common standard with their arch rivals.

Then there is the question of where the money comes from. The ANA asked that in 2024, and only 10% of marketers said retail media funding was incremental. So it’s coming from somewhere else. Some of it comes from trade spend, arguably an understandable and overdue update. But a lot of the new retail media investment is now coming directly out of brand-building budgets. Retailers know this, which is why they are increasingly reframing the investment up the funnel from purchase and toward the lofty, slushier world of awareness.

Attributing sales to people already inside your store, arriving ready to purchase your partner brands, is the single most flattering metric in marketing. Everything we know about growth, from Ehrenberg-Bass to Binet and Field, says it really comes from building mental availability among people who are not shopping your category today. Retail media, by its very definition and operation, reaches the ones who are.

After a disastrous decade of over-investment in performance marketing, American brands should be massively upping their brand-building efforts. Not stripping this budget for retail media requirements under the vague allusion that this is “brand building.”

None of which means they can or should walk away. Walmart is where America buys things. Ignoring its media is as dumb as ignoring its shelves. But treat its retail media requests for what they are: a bottom-of-the-funnel, defensive investment that locks in your distribution. And the correct updated destination for trade promotions.

But don’t think—for one moment—that it’s brand building.

Mark Ritson has a PhD in Marketing and spent 25 years working as a marketing professor, and has also worked as both a global brand consultant and as the in-house brand consultant for LVMH. His articles have appeared in the Sloan Management Review, Harvard Business Review, the Journal of Advertising and the Journal of Consumer Research.

In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, host Jennifer Rooney sits down with Jennifer Storms, chief marketing officer of NBCUniversal Television and Streaming, to break it down.

Jennifer traces her path from Olympic dreams to sports marketing to PepsiCo to NBCUniversal, sharing how NBCUniversal thinks about brand salience across NBC, Peacock, Bravo and NBC Sports.

She also discusses why the Olympics needed to be rebuilt as a year-round franchise, and how Legendary February turned three separate live events into one unified cultural moment.

Why a strong career north star should allow for strategic zigzags

How CPG experience shaped Jenny’s view of consumer behavior and brand building

Why brand salience matters when consumers have endless content choices

How NBCUniversal turns campaigns into year-round franchises

Why creators and athletes should be treated as storytellers, not just reach vehicles

How AI makes human storytelling and live experiences more valuable

Why live sports should be planned before, during and after the moment

Jennifer Storms is CMO of NBCUniversal Television and Streaming, where she leads brand strategy, integrated marketing, media and consumer engagement across NBC, Peacock, Bravo and NBC Sports. Her career spans the United States Olympic and Paralympic Committee, Turner Broadcasting, PepsiCo and NBCUniversal, giving her a rare perspective across sports, media, entertainment and consumer brands. At NBCUniversal, Jennifer focuses on building distinct brands, driving audience growth across platforms and turning major cultural moments into year-round franchises.

[07:14] Becoming a Chief Architect of Consumer Experience — At PepsiCo, Jennifer learned what it means to be the chief architect of consumer experience. That meant understanding not only what consumers need now, but what they will need next. It also meant standing in grocery and convenience stores, learning the realities of shelf space, linear feet and purchase behavior. That brand-side education now informs how she thinks about media, audience journeys and consumer connection at NBCUniversal.

[12:27] Why Brand Salience Matters in Streaming — With so many shows, platforms and brands inside NBCUniversal’s house of brands, Jennifer says the answer is not either/or. Consumers should connect with shows, but they should also have strong affinity for NBC, Peacock, Bravo and NBC Sports. The goal is brand salience: when someone sits down and wonders what they want to watch, NBCUniversal’s brands need to be top of mind. In a crowded streaming world, being remembered is half the battle.

Starting with the Olympics, then SNL and Legendary February, the team began treating major moments as enterprise growth opportunities that live beyond one season, one premiere or one live event. The goal is to keep the franchise alive in culture even when the show or event is not actively on.

Specialists matter, but so do people with varied experiences, different backgrounds, curiosity and the ability to shift across business needs. articles.title: Following Meta’s $17 Billion Settlement, Media Buyers Say: Don’t Touch That Dial
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg ADWEEK House: Advertising HQ brings the people shaping advertising, commerce, and media together for four days of unscripted conversations and after-hours connections. Meet us in Midtown, Oct. 5–8.

In the wake of Meta’s landmark $17 billion legal settlement on Wednesday, media buyers are cautioning against any abrupt shift in strategy, according to interviews with five agency executives.

Instead, brands and agencies should monitor the situation while keeping an eye on whether or not other social media platforms follow in Meta’s footsteps.

The company, which owns Facebook, Instagram, and Whatsapp, agreed to pay $12.7 billion in settlement fees, which would rise to around $18 billion if its peers at YouTube, Snapchat, and TikTok also implement the new restrictions it plans to adopt, which include a blackout period at night, notification limits during school hours, and a daily time limit of two hours.

One reason for this prudence is that the settlement does not affect the ad-buying mechanisms, according to Jack Johnston, vice president of innovation and growth at Tinuiti.

“This is not an advertising system change today,” Johnston said. “It is a potential audience supply change.”

Much of Meta’s value as an advertising platform comes from its sophisticated ad-targeting. Since it is unaffected in its structure, there is little reason to change course immediately, according to Ankit Jadav, associate director of paid social at Rain.

“Meta’s $18 billion child safety settlement doesn’t touch personalized targeting or our core buying mechanics,” Jadav said. “It’s about teen usage limits, not adtech.”

For agencies whose client base skews older, the settlement is close to a non-event, according to Andrew Becks, founder and CEO 301 Digital. Becks’ clients are largely targeting audiences over age 18, so the new restrictions have little direct impact on his buying operations.

But for brands trying to reach teens, the restrictions could drive up the price of that inventory.

“For brands that do market to younger audiences, this will certainly require a shift in strategy,” he said. “It may also drive costs to reach under 18s even higher, since there will likely be fewer overall ad impressions available from minors due to restrictions in the amount of time they’re allowed to spend on the platforms.”

FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context

That supply-side squeeze is where buyers with youth-adjacent clients expect the real impact to land. Categories including gaming, fast food, and fashion, which lean on teen-driven discovery, could be disproportionately affected, according to Jadav. Even then, the effects will likely be felt gradually.

“Expect a slow, delayed softening in reach/relevance rather than an immediate hit, likely showing up over 12 to 18 months—faster if TikTok, Snap, and YouTube follow suit,” said Jadav.

Nearly every buyer emphasized that same contingency. If these restrictions stay limited to Meta, the effect will be relatively isolated; if the other social platforms follow in its footsteps, this ruling could result in a larger shift in the paid media space.

“If the restrictions remain concentrated on Meta, some teen attention and advertiser investment may move to other platforms,” said Danielle Schultz, head of paid social at PMG. “If the settlement’s industry-wide adoption provisions lead to similar limits elsewhere, the total supply of teen social media inventory could contract.”

In the meantime, brands and agencies should note this moment as a baseline and compare against it in the coming months to monitor for any notable changes in cost or efficacy, three of the buyers advised.

Brands should document reach, frequency, CPM, placement, time of day, and conversion quality across the 13- to 17-year-old demographic and 18- to 24-year-old demographic, according to Schultz. They should also flag which campaigns lean most heavily on teen delivery or youth-led creator discovery.

Josh Rosenberg, co-founder and CEO of Day One Agency, framed the settlement as a reminder that brands and agencies should never rely too heavily on any single ecosystem.

“The smartest brands will build relationships that can travel with their audiences, rather than relationships that are dependent on any one platform or algorithm,” Rosenberg said.

articles.title: How to conduct a customer experience audit rooted in social intelligence
articles.fullContent:
Your customers are already telling you where their experience is falling short. The problem is, they don’t always tell you directly.

They post about it on social media, ask questions in comments, leave Google and Yelp reviews and talk about your brand in places your customer experience team may never see. Those conversations can expose frustrations, unmet needs and changing expectations that traditional feedback channels miss.

A customer experience audit gives you a structured way to evaluate those interactions across the customer journey. Building social intelligence into the process keeps the audit grounded in what customers are saying now and helps you decide what needs attention first.

In this article, we’ll break down what a customer experience audit involves, where social intelligence fits in and how to use the findings to improve the customer journey.

What is a customer experience audit?

A customer experience audit is a structured review of how people interact with your brand across the customer journey. It examines the touchpoints and feedback that shape the experience, from initial discovery through purchase and support.

Think of it like a health check for your customer experience. You’re looking at how different parts of the journey work together and where friction shows up between channels or departments.

A strong CX audit also looks beyond the channels your business owns. Social conversations and customer care interactions add context that surveys or CRM data alone may not capture, giving you a stronger foundation for what to improve.

5 steps for a modern customer experience audit that drives action

A customer experience audit works best when you approach it systematically. Here’s how to move from deciding what you want to learn to tracking whether your changes are working.

1. Set expectations for your CX audit

Before you pull data or review touchpoints, set the audit parameters. The steps below will help you establish what you’re trying to accomplish and what it will take to get there.

Involve the right stakeholders

Customer experience rarely sits with one department. Bring in people who own different parts of the journey, such as customer care, CX, social, marketing, PR and data analysts. Each group may catch gaps others miss.

Clarify everyone’s role upfront, too. Decide who will lead the audit, who will provide data or context and who needs to act on the findings.

Determine objectives and goals

Next, decide what you want to learn or improve. You might be trying to understand why customers abandon checkout after clicking through from social, improve response times on social or figure out where the brand experience feels inconsistent across channels.

Tie those objectives to specific parts of the customer journey and the outcomes that matter most. This will guide which touchpoints and metrics you review later.

Define scope

A CX audit can expand quickly across channels, customer groups and stages of the journey, so set boundaries before you begin.

Based on your objectives, decide what needs attention now based on your specific business priorities. That might mean auditing one priority audience across the full lifecycle or zeroing in on a stage where you already know there’s friction. Future audits can broaden the scope as new questions arise.

2. Map the customer journey across touch points

Customer journeys rarely follow a neat, predictable path. People move between channels and platforms as they discover brands, weigh their options and get support, making it harder to see the full experience in one place.

Mapping those touchpoints reveals how the pieces connect and where social media plays a role.

Capture the full customer lifecycle from discovery through care

Social influences customers at several key points in their relationship with your brand:

  • Product discovery: According to Sprout’s Q2 2026 Pulse Survey, around a third of consumers prefer social search for product reviews.
  • Purchase: Sprout’s State of Influencer Marketing Report found that 86% of consumers make an influencer-inspired purchase at least once a year.
  • Customer care: The Sprout Social Index™ found that 73% of social media users expect brands to respond on social within 24 hours.

Mapping your social media marketing funnel alongside the broader customer journey helps account for those interactions from discovery through ongoing social customer care.

Look beyond owned channels

Build your audit from the places customers interact with or talk about your brand. Alongside your own social posts and ads, include replies, DMs, chatbot interactions, reviews, customer posts, social shopping activity and traffic from social to your website. Widen the lens to review sites, discussion forums, influencer communities, media coverage and mentions that may never reach your profiles.

Sprout helps bring more of those touchpoints into one workflow. The Smart Inbox centralizes incoming social messages, while Reviews pulls customer feedback from sources including Google Business Profile, Yelp, Trustpilot and TripAdvisor. Sprout Social Listening bridges direct and indirect interactions, surfacing conversations about your brand and market that may not tag or mention you directly. Together, these tools give you a broader pool of customer conversations to draw from during the audit.

Connect social with the systems other teams use, too. The Sprout Social Salesforce integration enriches CRM profiles with social data, while Sprout’s Tableau BI Connector combines social with other business data for a fuller view of the journey.

3. Use social intelligence to identify pain points and gaps in customer experience

With the customer journey mapped, it’s time to diagnose what’s happening within it. Where is frustration building? What questions keep coming up? Are expectations changing faster than your experience can keep pace with?

Social intelligence helps answer those questions by illustrating how customer sentiment and conversation patterns are changing across the market.

Analyze audience sentiment

Look at how customers feel at key points in the journey. A drop in sentiment around a product launch or an increase in negative customer care messages can point to experiences worth investigating.

Social listening helps track sentiment across broader conversations, while Sprout’s Sentiment for Messages classifies incoming messages and reviews, enabling teams to identify interactions that need attention. NewsWhip by Sprout Social further adds predictive media intelligence to indicate when stories or issues are gaining traction.

articles.title: OpenAI Adds WebMCP Site Tools To ChatGPT’s Browser via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
OpenAI is adding WebMCP support to the built-in browser in its ChatGPT desktop app, letting websites expose actions that ChatGPT and Codex can use directly from the page.

This is separate from the server-based Model Context Protocol support ChatGPT has offered since 2025. WebMCP lets the webpage you’re visiting provide tools automatically, without setting up a separate MCP connector.

Site tools assist with tasks like searching documents, editing files, exploring dashboards, comparing travel options, and updating shopping carts. The selection of tools varies depending on the website, so options might differ from page to page.

An arrow appears in the address bar when site tools are available, showing whether a tool can read data or make changes. ChatGPT can automatically find a suitable tool, which remains linked to the page where it was accessed and disappears when you close that page.

Without site tools, ChatGPT uses its standard browser capabilities, such as clicking and typing. WebMCP offers developers an additional choice. It’s different from the server-based Model Context Protocol, or MCP, which links an AI application to a local or remote server and can operate without an open webpage.

WebMCP makes available specific tools from the webpage the agent is visiting. A webpage can register JavaScript functions as tools, including their names, descriptions, and structured input schemas.

OpenAI shared this goal in its challenge announcement:

“Instead of leaving agents to guess their way through your UI, you define exactly how they can use your app.”

Site tools operate within the current page and signed-in session. Developers can connect them to existing application logic and permissions.

OpenAI calls WebMCP an experimental open standard. The specification is a draft from the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group and isn’t on the W3C Standards Track.

Site tools are accessible within the built-in browser of the ChatGPT desktop app when available for an account. According to OpenAI’s documentation, this feature requires GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra; GPT-5.6 Luna has WebMCP disabled. Site tools aren’t available in Enterprise or Edu workspaces.

Access depends on rollout status and available tools. Although the feature doesn’t work in Chrome via ChatGPT, developers can test WebMCP in Chrome by enabling an experimental flag or joining its origin trial . Some websites might not support site tools, and embedded content may lack these tools. Tools used on one page won’t automatically be available on others.

Site tools can work while you’re signed in and might change website data. OpenAI asks for your permission before ChatGPT interacts with a site and confirms actions like making purchases, deleting data, changing account settings, sending messages, or sharing personal info.

They also warn about risks such as data exfiltration and prompt injection. While each tool invocation receives a safety review, these checks don’t guarantee the website or its responses are trustworthy. Previously, SEJ reported that Chrome’s guidance identifies malicious tool descriptions and contaminated outputs as prompt-injection risks for browser-based agents.

SEJ mentioned back in May that Google’s website guidelines encourage designing sites that are agent-friendly. Now, OpenAI has added WebMCP support to ChatGPT’s desktop browser. This new feature lets website managers choose which actions are available, rather than depending solely on ChatGPT.

While WebMCP gives sites a structured way to expose actions to agents, the documentation doesn’t explain how it might affect rankings, citations, or discoverability.

Key takeaways

  1. Facebook ad targeting offers four main audience types (Core, Custom, Lookalike, and Advantage+), each suited to different campaign goals and data sources.
  2. Advantage+ audience targeting uses Meta’s AI to find high-converting audiences automatically, often lowering cost per conversion by double digits compared to manual targeting alone.
  3. Privacy changes have reduced some manual targeting options, making first-party data like customer lists and Pixel data more valuable than ever for precise targeting.
  4. Matching your targeting approach to your budget and creative quality matters as much as the audience settings themselves.

What is Facebook ad targeting?

Facebook ad targeting is the system within Meta Ads Manager that lets advertisers define exactly who sees your ads. Instead of showing your ad to all 3.56 billion daily active people across Meta’s apps, you choose audiences based on characteristics like age, location, interests, past interactions with your business, or similarities to your best customers.

The platform offers four main approaches:

  • Core audiences (detailed targeting): Manually select demographics, interests, and behaviors.
  • Custom audiences: Retarget people who already know your business using your own data.
  • Lookalike audiences: Find new people who resemble your existing customers.
  • Advantage+ audiences: Let Meta’s AI automatically find the best audience for your campaign.

Bonus: Use our free Facebook Ads budget calculato r to figure out exactly how much you need to spend to get the results you want. Let us do the math for you!

How does Facebook ad targeting work?

Facebook ad targeting works through Meta’s ad auction. Your audience settings don’t buy placements directly. Instead, they define the pool of people your ad is eligible to reach, and then every available impression within that pool goes to auction against other advertisers competing for the same person.

Meta decides the winner using a total value score built from several inputs:

  • Audience settings: Who you’ve made your ad eligible to reach, whether that’s a Core audience, a Custom Audience, or a broad Advantage+ pool.
  • Your bid: How much you’re willing to pay for the outcome you’ve selected, set manually or by Meta’s automated bidding.
  • Estimated action rates: How likely Meta thinks a specific person is to take your chosen action, based on their past behavior and your campaign’s conversion history.
  • Ad quality and relevance: Signals from your creative, engagement history, and feedback from people who have seen similar ads.

The practical takeaway: your audience settings are only one lever. A tightly defined audience paired with weak creative will still lose auctions to a broader audience paired with strong creative, because Meta’s system is optimizing for the outcome, not the input.

Better targeting means higher relevance scores, lower costs, and stronger ROI, especially as average ad prices rose 9% in 2025. The rest of this guide covers each option in detail, plus the strategies that help enterprise teams get the most from their ad spend.

What are the Facebook ad targeting options?

Meta gives advertisers several layers of targeting to work with, from broad demographic filters to AI-powered audience optimization. Understanding what each type does, and when to use it, is the foundation of any effective campaign.

Here’s how the four main targeting types compare:

Core audiences (detailed targeting)

Core audiences are what most people think of when they picture Facebook ad targeting. You manually build an audience by selecting criteria across three pillars: demographics, interests, and behaviors.

Demographics let you filter by:

  • Age: Target specific age ranges, from teenagers to seniors.
  • Gender: Choose men, women, or all genders.
  • Education: Reach people based on educational background, from high school graduates to advanced degree holders.
  • Job title: Target professionals in specific industries or roles relevant to your products or services.
  • Location: Filter by country, state, city, or zip code.

Interests let you reach people based on their hobbies and affinities, such as fitness, travel, cooking, or specific brands they follow. Facebook interest targeting pulls from pages people have liked, content they engage with, and related topics.

Behaviors target users based on their actions, including shopping habits, device usage, travel frequency, and purchase history.

Use case: If you’re promoting a new line of fitness apparel, you might target women aged 25-40 who live in urban areas and have shown an interest in fitness-related pages.

Put Trellis on the time-consuming stuff

You didn’t get into social to spend your days pulling data, cleaning reports and packaging up findings for other people to act on.

That’s where Trellis can help.

Trellis is available on every account and every plan of the core Sprout product, with no upgrade needed. During Breaking Ground, we shared five workflows that can help take some of the manual work off your plate, along with the prompts you can use to get started.

Here’s one of the most popular examples from the session. You can also visit Sprout Academy for  more ways to put Trellis to work .

Turn performance data into an executive summary

You know the question: How did the campaign perform? 

Giving a useful answer can mean moving between numerous dashboards and spreadsheets.  The summary may take only a few minutes to read, but it took you hours to assemble.

Instead, try asking Trellis:

Trellis Prompt:

“Review our publishing data from the last 14 days and summarize the top 3 creative themes that drove the highest engagement. Summarize this for an executive audience.”

 

Back comes three creative drivers with the posts that prove each one, written with an executive audience in mind. You bring the context and judgement; Trellis gives you a better starting point.

More ways to make the work flow

Of course, AI can only save you time when it’s connected to the work you’re already doing. This quarter’s updates extend well beyond Trellis. Here’s what else shipped across the platform.

The more networks and content types your team manages, the easier it is for conversations and data to become scattered. These updates bring more of that activity into your existing workflows.

This article breaks down which tasks are best handed off to AI, where human judgment still matters and how automation can give social teams more room to focus on higher-value work.

Social media manager tasks: A daily overview

A social media manager’s day covers a lot more than planning content and hitting publish. Here are some social media tasks that fall under most social media job titles:

  • Analyze metrics to gauge performance
  • Brainstorm content ideas
  • Research trending topics and conversations
  • Manage paid social media campaigns

  • Handle crisis communication, as needed

Which of these are you still doing manually? Look at each task and ask: Could AI handle it? Or does it still need a person’s judgment?

Automated tasks in social media marketing: What AI can do now

A few years ago, most social media tasks required a person at every step. Now, AI handles a growing share of the daily workload, from scheduling to reporting to the first pass on customer replies.

Here’s where it’s already doing the heavy lifting.

Publishing & scheduling

Getting a post approved and published can often involve a few rounds of email or Slack follow-ups with your manager or other stakeholders. Automated approval workflows remove that back-and-forth by sending content directly to the right person at the right stage.

Choosing when to post has also become more precise. Instead of relying on generic best-practice windows, AI can analyze when your specific audience is most likely to engage. Sprout’s Optimal Send Times with ViralPost uses your audience’s behavior to recommend the best publishing times.

Alt text is another task that can slip when deadlines get tight. AI can help by generating descriptive alt text within the publishing workflow, making accessibility easier to build into the process. Sprout’s Generate ALT Text capability does this directly in the platform.

AI can cut down that work by letting teams query social data in plain language instead of rebuilding the analysis from scratch each time. With Sprout’s Trellis, social teams, leaders and cross-functional partners can ask questions about social performance and get answers without waiting for someone to pull a report.

That also makes social data more accessible and useful outside the social team. If someone in product or customer care wants to know how a launch went or understand customer sentiment, they can get the answer directly by asking an AI agent.

Social listening & media intelligence

Thousands of conversations can unfold around your brand, competitors and industry in a matter of hours. AI helps teams sort through that volume by analyzing conversations for patterns, shifts in sentiment and emerging topics that would be difficult to catch manually.

Within Sprout Listening, Trellis takes that a step further by letting teams ask questions about sentiment, share of voice or emerging themes in plain language and get answers based on their listening data.

It can also draft responses for customer care agents to review and personalize, accelerating personalization while cutting down the time spent writing routine replies from scratch.

Automating routine work gives social teams more time for the parts of the job that depend on judgment, context and relationships.

Getting another team to act on social insights takes more than sending them a report. Social leaders need to understand what product, customer care or sales is trying to solve, then connect social data to the decisions already on their plate.

articles.title: The Practical Guide to Google Analytics 4
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Google renamed “Conversions” to “Key Events” in 2024. The terms mean different things in GA4 and Google Ads, so getting the terminology right matters when comparing numbers across platforms. 
  • Every interaction in GA4 is event-based, with parameters providing the context behind what happened.
  • Data-driven attribution is GA4’s default model, using machine learning to spread credit across all the touchpoints that led to a conversion. 
  • BigQuery export is free for standard properties and unlocks analysis that the standard reports can’t handle. 
  • DebugView is the fastest way to catch broken tracking before it becomes weeks of unusable data.

Are you getting the most out of Google Analytics 4 (GA4)?

GA4 has been Google’s standard analytics platform for a few years now. The move from Universal Analytics (UA) was a major shift, but Google has continued updating GA4 itself along the way. One of the biggest changes came in 2024, when Google replaced “Conversions” with “Key Events” in 2024. 

While some marketers might miss UA, there’s no going back.

This GA4 guide skips the history lesson and focuses on what you need to do in GA4 day to day, from proper setup to tracking key events (not conversions) and other impactful metrics.

What Is Google Analytics 4?

Google Analytics 4 is the current version of Google Analytics, and it provides web analytics on a level that allows marketers to effectively analyze important customer usage metrics, not just track traffic.

Before we get into the details, here’s a quick Google Analytics 4 overview. 

Google Analytics 4 tracks the entire customer path across multiple platforms and leverages AI and machine learning to provide more detailed insights into how users interact with your website and app.

GA4 combines cross-channel measurement and AI-driven predictive analytics. It also operates under a privacy-first tracking framework designed for today’s privacy laws, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). 

These features combine to give marketers a more complete view of how users interact with their digital properties than what UA offered.

How to Set Up Google Analytics 4

Many marketers ask me how to use GA4. Your setup process will depend on whether you’re tracking a website or an app (or both). I’ve broken down each option below.

Google Analytics for Firebase

Firebase is Google’s app development platform that helps you build and deploy apps and games. If you enable Google Analytics when creating a Firebase project, Firebase automatically links your app to a GA4 property.  

If you’re working with an older Firebase project, you may need to link it to a GA4 property or complete Google’s upgrade process.

To upgrade your Firebase account to Google Analytics 4, follow these steps:

  1. Log in to the Firebase console.
  2. Go to Analytics > Dashboard on the left panel.
  3. Follow any prompts to enable or upgrade GA for the project. 

Once linked, you can find app analytics in both the Firebase console and Google Analytics.

Setting up Google Analytics 4 from Scratch

If you’ve never used Google Analytics before or you want to set up a brand-new website, you’ll need to start from scratch:

  • Create an Analytics account if you haven’t already by visiting https://analytics.google.com and opening Admin. Then click Create, and then Account (skip if you already have an account).
  • In the Property column, click Create > Property.
  • Enter a name for your new property, and select a time zone and currency. 
  • Select your industry category and business size.
  • Select your business objectives (e.g., “Get baseline reports,” “Generate leads”).
  • Click Create and accept the Terms of Service.
  • Add a data stream (Web, iOS, or Android) to start collecting data.

Source: https://www.eridesignstudio.com/insights/set-up-a-google-analytics-4-property/

A data stream is a source of information that feeds your GA4 analytics property. It could be your website or your app. Google will guide you through adding each data stream.

Install With Google Tag Manager

For most marketers, Google Tag Manager (GTM) is the recommended installation method. GTM lets you deploy and update the GA4 tag (along with other marketing tags) without touching the site code whenever something changes.

To set up, create a free GTM account and add a container for your site. Google will give you two snippets of code to paste on every page (one in the <head>, one right after the opening <body> tag). 

Once the container is live, create a Google tag inside GTM using your GA4 Measurement ID and set it to fire on all pages. Publish the container to push your changes live.

Verify With DebugView

After setup, use DebugView (found under Admin) to confirm your events are firing correctly. It shows real-time event data from a single device with debug mode enabled, which beats waiting for reports to populate. Skipping this step is a common way for broken tracking to go unnoticed for weeks.

If your competitive research involves jumping between LinkedIn, G2, and an overgrown collection of bookmarked pricing pages, there’s a better way.

Competitive intelligence software automates the detective work, surfacing the competitor moves that actually matter. 

Let’s take a closer look at the best platforms for tracking competitors across sales, search, social, and beyond.

  2. There’s no one-size-fits-all tool. The right pick depends on whether you’re tracking deals, website traffic, or brand chatter.
  3. Test it inside your real workflow. If a tool requires constant cleanup or five new steps, it’s not worth it.

What is competitive intelligence software?

Competitive intelligence software is a tool that helps companies monitor competitors and turn external information into business insights.

For example, marketing teams might use it to see which keywords a rival is ranking for, while product development teams might use it to catch new features early.

You could do all of this manually, but that means refreshing competitor websites, pricing pages, and review sites on repeat. These tools bring those signals into one place, so you can spend more time deciding your next steps.

What kinds of competitor data does it track?

Most competitive intelligence tools monitor some mix of the following:

  • Pricing changes: A new tier, a sudden discount, or a reshuffled package can tell you a lot about who a competitor is trying to win over.
  • Product launches and messaging shifts: Catch new features, positioning pivots, and changes in how competitors talk about their value.
  • Web traffic and SEO performance: Track which keywords competitors are winning, where their traffic comes from, and which parts of their site are pulling the most weight.
  • Social share of voice and sentiment: Find out who’s dominating the conversation online (and whether that conversation is positive, negative, or somewhere in between).
  • Reviews and community chatter: Buyers are pretty honest on sites like G2 and Reddit. That candor is gold when you’re sizing up the competition.
  • Hiring activity: Job postings can be surprisingly revealing. A sudden hiring spree in AI, enterprise sales, or a new region can hint at what’s coming next.
  • Company news and funding: Leadership changes, acquisitions, earnings transcripts, and funding rounds often signal big moves before they show up in the product.

No single tool tracks all of this equally well, which is why the best pick depends on what your team actually needs to watch. More on that next.

What are the main types of competitive intelligence software?

Competitive intelligence software falls into four main types: all-in-one platforms, sales enablement tools, digital market intelligence tools, and social and brand intelligence tools. Here’s how they compare:

All-in-one competitive intelligence platforms

These platforms try to cover the whole competitive picture. They pull together signals like competitor news and product updates, then package them into competitor profiles, alerts, and digests for your team.

These tools are a good fit when:

  • You want one central home for competitive intel
  • Multiple teams (sales, product, marketing) all need access to the same insights
  • You’d rather get a weekly digest than dig for updates yourself

But, the trade-off: All-in-one tools cover a lot of ground, but specialized tools usually dig deeper in their specific lane.

Sales enablement platforms

Sales enablement tools are built for the moment a competitor comes up in a deal. They arm reps with battlecards, win/loss insights, and objection-handling answers. They typically integrate with CRMs like Salesforce.

Digital market intelligence

These tools track how competitors perform online, which makes them a favorite for marketing and growth teams.

Most cover:

  • Traffic estimates: How much traffic competitors get and which channels drive it
  • SEO and keyword research: What they rank for, where they’re gaining ground, and which gaps might be yours for the taking
  • Paid ads: Where competitors are spending and what their ads look like
  • Referral sources: Which websites, partners, and platforms are sending them visitors, plus the quality of their backlinks.

Social and brand intelligence

These tools handle social media monitoring at scale, tracking how people talk about your competitors (and you) across social media, blogs, forums, and review sites.

These tools typically cover:

  • Share of voice: How much of the online conversation your brand owns
  • Sentiment analysis: Whether that conversation is positive, negative, or somewhere in the middle
  • Trend detection: Topics gaining steam in your market before they peak

articles.title: What is social media monitoring? Full 2026 guide
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media monitoring is the practice of tracking brand mentions, keywords, and conversations across social platforms to understand what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.
  2. Monitoring helps teams catch reputation risks early, respond to customers faster, and surface insights that inform marketing, product, and sales decisions.
  3. AI-powered monitoring tools can now analyze sentiment, detect crises, and surface trends across millions of sources in real time.
  4. The best monitoring strategies share insights across the organization, not just the social team, and measure ROI tied to business outcomes.

What is social media monitoring?

Social media monitoring is the process of tracking what people are saying about your brand on social media.

This includes both tagged and untagged mentions, whether they show up in comments on your own accounts or in conversations happening elsewhere across the social web.

In practice, that scope is wider than most teams expect. Monitoring covers posts, comments, replies, reviews, video captions, forum threads, and news coverage across networks like Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and Bluesky, where 84% of U.S. adults use YouTube and 71% use Facebook. Most of those conversations never tag your handle, which is exactly why manual checking falls short.

Bonus !!!

Take action on customer insights and drive impact for your organization with our complete guide to social listening using Hootsuite x Talkwalker.

Download now

How does social media monitoring work?

Social media monitoring isn’t just one activity. It’s a mix of signals that, together, tell you what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.

Here are the key components that make up social media monitoring:

  • Brand mentions: Track when people talk about your brand across comments, posts, and conversations. This is your baseline signal, and it covers both direct tags and untagged references.
  • Sentiment analysis: Understand how people feel about your brand by looking at whether mentions are positive, negative, or neutral. Tracked over time, sentiment tells you whether perception is improving or slipping.
  • Competitor analysis: Keep tabs on what people are saying about your competitors, including their campaigns, products, and gaps. Their weak spots are often your opportunities.
  • Industry trends: Follow larger conversations in your industry, including trending topics, hashtags, and viral moments, so you can join them while they still matter.
  • Influencer identification: Find people already talking about your brand who could become partners or advocates. Existing fans usually convert into partnerships faster than cold outreach.
  • Share of voice (SOV): Measure how much of the conversation your brand owns compared to competitors. It’s one of the clearest ways to benchmark visibility.
  • Crisis detection: Catch spikes in mentions or shifts in sentiment early, so you can respond before things escalate.
  • Hashtag tracking: Monitor how your branded hashtags, campaign tags, and industry keywords are performing.
  • AI-powered analysis: Use AI to cluster themes, flag anomalies, and summarize what thousands of mentions add up to, instead of reading them one by one.

Together, these signals turn everyday social conversations into actionable insights for your team.

Social media monitoring vs. social listening: what’s the difference?

The short answer: monitoring tracks individual conversations as they happen, and social listening analyzes those conversations in aggregate to find patterns. They’re closely related, but they serve different purposes.

  • Social monitoring is reactive. It focuses on tracking mentions and responding to what’s happening in real time.
  • Social listening is proactive. It starts by analyzing the information from social monitoring to spot larger patterns and trends. In other words, it looks at the bigger picture to improve your social media marketing strategy over time.

What is a social media SWOT analysis?

A social media SWOT analysis is a framework marketers use to evaluate their social media performance by looking at four areas: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.

Here are a few scenarios where a social media SWOT analysis could come in handy:

  • Deciding whether to join a new social media platform
  • Rebranding or repositioning
